## Why these two chapters go together

Chapters 16 and 17 aren't new ideas — they're **the same toolkit you already have** (bootstrapping, randomization, the normal model, hypothesis tests, confidence intervals), applied first to **one** proportion, then to the **difference between two** proportions.

. . .

- **Ch. 16 (one proportion):** review of everything from Ch. 11-13, plus one genuinely new tool — figuring out **how big a sample you need** before collecting data.

. . .

- **Ch. 17 (two proportions):** the same machinery, extended to comparing two groups — which means one new wrinkle in how we compute the standard error.

## Recap: one proportion, three ways

For a single proportion $\hat p$, you already know three ways to get a p-value or CI:

| Method | Tool |
|---|---|
| Simulation (null true) | randomization / null simulation |
| Simulation (no null assumed) | bootstrapping |
| Mathematical model | $Z = \dfrac{\hat p - p_0}{SE}$, $\ SE = \sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ |

All three answer the same question — they just make different tradeoffs between speed, transparency, and required conditions (independence; for the normal model, also $np\ge10$ and $n(1-p)\ge10$).

## New idea: how big a sample do I need?

Every confidence interval has a margin of error, $ME = z^\star \times SE$. Instead of computing $ME$ *after* collecting data, we can flip the formula around **before** collecting data, to plan a sample size.

. . .

::: {.callout-note title="Sample size for a desired margin of error"}
$$n = \left(\frac{z^\star}{ME}\right)^2 p(1-p)$$
If you have no prior estimate of $p$, use $p=0.5$ — this is the most conservative choice, since $p(1-p)$ is maximized at $p=0.5$, giving the largest (safest) $n$.
:::

## Worked example: planning a sample size

> Researchers want to estimate the satisfaction rate for a new tutoring program to within a margin of error of 3%, at 95% confidence, with no prior estimate of the true rate.

. . .
 
$$n = \left(\frac{1.96}{0.03}\right)^2 (0.5)(0.5) = (65.33)^2 (0.25) \approx 1067.1$$

**Always round up:** $n = 1068$. Rounding down would give a margin of error very slightly *larger* than what was promised.

. . .

# Two proportions

## Comparing two groups: what changes?

Now we have two independent samples, and we care about the **difference** $p_1 - p_2$. The point estimate is simple: $\hat p_1 - \hat p_2$. The standard error is where it gets interesting — and it depends on *what question you're asking*.

. . .

- **Building a confidence interval?** Use each group's own $\hat p$ — the **unpooled** SE.

. . .

- **Testing $H_0: p_1 = p_2$?** Under that null, both groups are assumed to share one common proportion — so we should estimate that *shared* rate first, using **all** the data. This is the **pooled** SE.

## The two standard errors

::: {.callout-note title="Unpooled SE (for a confidence interval)"}
$$SE = \sqrt{\frac{\hat p_1(1-\hat p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat p_2(1-\hat p_2)}{n_2}}$$
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-note title="Pooled SE (for a hypothesis test of $H_0: p_1=p_2$)"}
$$\hat p_{pool} = \frac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2}, \qquad SE = \sqrt{\hat p_{pool}(1-\hat p_{pool})\left(\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}\right)}$$
:::

. . .

**Why the difference matters:** under $H_0$, we're assuming one shared truth — so we should estimate the SE consistently with that assumption, not by trusting each sample's own (possibly different) $\hat p$.

## Success-failure condition, twice over

Just like the one-proportion case, the normal model requires large enough samples — now checked **separately for each group**, using the pooled proportion when testing $H_0$:

. . .

$$n_1 \hat p_{pool} \ge 10, \quad n_1(1-\hat p_{pool}) \ge 10, \quad n_2 \hat p_{pool} \ge 10, \quad n_2(1-\hat p_{pool}) \ge 10$$

## Case study: disaggregating tobacco use

A 2021 study (Rao et al.) examined current smoking rates among different Asian American subgroups, rather than lumping them together — a good example of why disaggregating categories can matter.

|              | Asian-Indian | Chinese |
|--------------|:---:|:---:|
| $n$          | 4,373 | 4,736 |
| smokers      | 223   | 279   |
| $\hat p$     | 0.0510 | 0.0589 |

> Is the smoking rate among Asian-Indian Americans different from the rate among Chinese Americans?

. . . 

$H_0: p_{Indian} = p_{Chinese}$ vs. $H_A: p_{Indian} \ne p_{Chinese}$ (two-sided, by default).

## Running the test

$$\hat p_{pool} = \frac{223+279}{4373+4736} = \frac{502}{9109} \approx 0.0551$$
. . .

$$SE_{pool} = \sqrt{0.0551(0.9449)\left(\frac{1}{4373}+\frac{1}{4736}\right)} \approx 0.00479$$

. . .

$$Z = \frac{0.0510 - 0.0589}{0.00479} \approx -1.65 \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad p\text{-value} \approx 0.098$$

. . .

Since $0.098 > 0.05$, we **fail to reject $H_0$** — this sample doesn't provide convincing evidence of a difference between these two groups' smoking rates.

## Now the confidence interval

For the CI, switch to the **unpooled** SE (each group keeps its own $\hat p$):

. . .

$$SE_{unpooled} = \sqrt{\frac{0.0510(0.9490)}{4373} + \frac{0.0589(0.9411)}{4736}} \approx 0.00477$$

. . .


$$(\hat p_1 - \hat p_2) \pm 1.96 \times SE = -0.0079 \pm 1.96(0.00477) = (-0.0173,\ 0.0014)$$

. . .

**Consistency check:** the interval contains 0 — matching our "fail to reject" conclusion from the test. This will always line up, since both are built from essentially the same logic.

## In code

```r
# Two-proportion test/CI in R -- same function you've already used
prop.test(x = c(223, 279), n = c(4373, 4736))
```

`prop.test()` handles the pooled/unpooled distinction internally — it's using the pooled SE to get the p-value, and (a version close to) the unpooled SE for the reported confidence interval, all in one call.

## Wrapping up

- Chapters 16 and 17 don't introduce a new *kind* of thinking — they're the same simulation/CLT/hypothesis-testing framework from Ch. 11-14, applied to one proportion and then to two.

. . .

- The one genuinely new tool: **planning sample size in advance**, using $n = (z^\star/ME)^2\, p(1-p)$.

. . .

- The one genuinely new wrinkle: **pooled vs. unpooled SE** when comparing two proportions — pool when your null hypothesis assumes one shared truth, don't pool when you're just trying to estimate two separate quantities.

. . .

- Next: this exact same one-vs-two-group structure repeats again for **means** — that's what the t-test extensions to two samples will look like.
